subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 45-year-old man presents with acute onset of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back after a weekend of heavy alcohol use. Vital signs are stable. Serum lipase is 6 times the upper limit of normal, and CT shows peripancreatic edema with few small fluid collections.
question: Which of the following best describes the diagnostic criteria used to make this diagnosis?

options.text: A single criterion is sufficient when the pain is characteristic
At least 2 of 3: characteristic pain, lipase at least 3 times the upper limit of normal, and characteristic imaging
Characteristic pain and imaging, with a normal lipase required
All 3 criteria are mandatory; 2 of 3 is insufficient
Lipase alone is sufficient when imaging is negative

explanation_correct: Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed when 2 of 3 criteria are present: acute epigastric pain often radiating to the back, serum amylase or lipase at least 3 times the upper limit of normal, and characteristic imaging findings. Lipase is more specific than amylase. This patient satisfies all three criteria, which is more than the required two. The underlying mechanism is autodigestion of the pancreas by pancreatic enzymes, and the process is usually sterile.

explanation_incorrect.A: One criterion alone is not enough; the standard requires at least two of the three findings.
explanation_incorrect.C: Lipase is not required to be normal; an elevated lipase is itself one of the diagnostic criteria and is more specific than amylase.
explanation_incorrect.D: All three findings are not mandatory; meeting any two of the three establishes the diagnosis.
explanation_incorrect.E: A single elevated lipase is not sufficient by itself, and imaging is not required when the pain and enzyme criteria are both present.

educationalObjective: Acute pancreatitis requires 2 of 3 criteria: characteristic epigastric pain radiating to the back, lipase or amylase at least 3 times normal, and typical imaging.
source: Generated from 9. Gastrointestinal.pdf - Pathology: Acute and chronic pancreatitis

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 39-year-old man with no history of alcohol use or gallstones presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. Laboratory studies show lipase 8 times the upper limit of normal and serum triglycerides of 1,800 mg/dL. He reports no trauma, no scorpion exposure, and takes no medications.
question: Which cause of acute pancreatitis is most likely in this patient?

options.text: Gallstone disease
Ethanol use
Scorpion sting
Hypertriglyceridemia above 1000 mg/dL
Autoimmune disease

explanation_correct: The causes of acute pancreatitis are recalled by I GET SMASHED: Idiopathic, Gallstones, Ethanol, Trauma, Steroids, Mumps, Autoimmune disease, Scorpion sting, Hypercalcemia or Hypertriglyceridemia above 1000 mg/dL, ERCP, and Drugs such as sulfa drugs, NRTIs, and protease inhibitors. This patient has extreme hypertriglyceridemia well above the threshold with no other trigger, making that the cause. Autodigestion by pancreatic enzymes then produces the typical pain and enzyme elevation.

explanation_incorrect.A: Gallstone pancreatitis would be supported by a history of stones and often cholestatic enzyme abnormalities; none are present here.
explanation_incorrect.B: Ethanol is a common cause of pancreatitis overall, but the patient denies alcohol use and has a clear alternative trigger.
explanation_incorrect.C: Scorpion sting is a rare, geographically limited cause and there is no reported exposure in this patient.
explanation_incorrect.E: Autoimmune pancreatitis is a distinct process and would not explain a triglyceride level of 1,800 mg/dL in an otherwise well patient.

educationalObjective: Hypertriglyceridemia above 1000 mg/dL is a recognized cause of acute pancreatitis within the I GET SMASHED mnemonic.
source: Generated from 9. Gastrointestinal.pdf - Pathology: Acute and chronic pancreatitis

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 52-year-old woman is recovering from an episode of acute gallstone pancreatitis. Six weeks later, CT shows a well-circumscribed fluid collection adjacent to the pancreas with a smooth enhancing rim but no epithelial lining.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this collection?

options.text: Pancreatic pseudocyst lined by granulation tissue rather than epithelium
Pancreatic abscess lined by intestinal epithelium
Acute peripancreatic edema that will resolve without follow-up
Pancreatic adenocarcinoma arising within a chronic fluid collection
Splenic subcapsular hematoma from pancreatic enzyme erosion

explanation_correct: A pancreatic pseudocyst is a localized collection of pancreatic fluid and enzymes walled off by granulation tissue, explicitly not by epithelium; this is why it is called a pseudocyst. It is a well-known local complication of acute pancreatitis. Other complications include abscess, parenchymal or peripancreatic necrosis, hemorrhage, infection, organ failure such as ALI/ARDS, shock and renal failure, and hypocalcemia from calcium soap precipitation.

explanation_incorrect.B: An abscess is an infected pus-filled collection and is not lined by intestinal epithelium; it is not the expected finding six weeks after uncomplicated pancreatitis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Acute peripancreatic edema occurs early and resolves; a persistent, well-encapsulated collection six weeks later is a pseudocyst.
explanation_incorrect.D: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma is a ductal tumor with disorganized glands and cellular infiltration, not a fluid collection with a granulation tissue wall.
explanation_incorrect.E: A splenic hematoma would be a blood collection in the spleen, not a peripancreatic collection with a granulation tissue rim following pancreatitis.

educationalObjective: A pancreatic pseudocyst is a complication of acute pancreatitis lined by granulation tissue, not by epithelium.
source: Generated from 9. Gastrointestinal.pdf - Pathology: Acute and chronic pancreatitis

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 58-year-old man with severe acute pancreatitis has persistent hypotension and requires mechanical ventilation. On hospital day 3, his serum calcium falls to 7.1 mg/dL with a normal albumin. He has no history of parathyroid disease, vitamin D deficiency, or diuretic use.
question: Which mechanism best explains this patient's hypocalcemia?

options.text: Parathyroid gland destruction by circulating pancreatic enzymes
Increased renal calcium excretion caused by loop diuretics
Reduced intestinal calcium absorption from chronic pancreatic insufficiency
Dilutional hypocalcemia from aggressive normal saline resuscitation
Precipitation of calcium soaps from lipase-mediated fat necrosis

explanation_correct: Hypocalcemia in acute pancreatitis results from precipitation of calcium soaps as pancreatic lipase causes fat necrosis and free fatty acids bind calcium. It is a marker of severe disease and commonly accompanies systemic complications such as ALI/ARDS, shock, and renal failure. The abrupt fall during an episode of severe pancreatitis with normal albumin and no other cause makes saponification the correct mechanism.

explanation_incorrect.A: Parathyroid destruction is not a recognized complication of pancreatitis; the parathyroid glands are not exposed to pancreatic enzymes in the neck.
explanation_incorrect.B: Loop diuretics do increase renal calcium excretion, but no diuretic is described and this is a classic acute pancreatitis complication.
explanation_incorrect.C: Impaired intestinal absorption produces gradual, chronic hypocalcemia rather than an abrupt decline on hospital day 3.
explanation_incorrect.D: Large-volume saline can dilute calcium modestly, but severe hypocalcemia in this setting reflects calcium soap formation from fat necrosis.

educationalObjective: Hypocalcemia in severe acute pancreatitis is caused by precipitation of calcium soaps during fat necrosis and signals severe disease.
source: Generated from 9. Gastrointestinal.pdf - Pathology: Acute and chronic pancreatitis

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 55-year-old man with a long history of alcohol use disorder presents with steatorrhea, weight loss, and new-onset diabetes mellitus. Imaging shows a shrunken, calcified pancreas with atrophic ducts. Serum amylase and lipase are within normal limits.
question: Which of the following best explains these findings?

options.text: Acute pancreatitis with transient exocrine suppression
Pancreatic adenocarcinoma with obstruction of the main pancreatic duct
Chronic pancreatitis with exocrine and endocrine insufficiency
Celiac disease with villous atrophy and malabsorption
Primary bile acid deficiency from terminal ileal disease

explanation_correct: Chronic pancreatitis is characterized by chronic inflammation, atrophy, and calcification of the pancreas, with alcohol use disorder as the major risk factor; genetic causes include cystic fibrosis and SPINK1 mutations. When pancreatic function falls below about 10%, exocrine insufficiency causes steatorrhea and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, and endocrine insufficiency causes diabetes mellitus. Unlike acute pancreatitis, amylase and lipase may be normal. Chronic pancreatitis can also produce pseudocysts.

explanation_incorrect.A: Acute pancreatitis typically presents with severe pain and markedly elevated lipase, almost always elevated, rather than a calcified atrophic gland with normal enzymes.
explanation_incorrect.B: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma can cause weight loss and diabetes, but a shrunken calcified pancreas with normal enzymes points to chronic pancreatitis instead.
explanation_incorrect.D: Celiac disease causes steatorrhea from villous atrophy but does not produce pancreatic calcification or pancreatic diabetes.
explanation_incorrect.E: Terminal ileal disease causes bile acid malabsorption and diarrhea, not a calcified atrophic pancreas with exocrine and endocrine failure.

educationalObjective: Chronic pancreatitis causes atrophy and calcification with steatorrhea, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, and diabetes once function falls below 10%, and enzymes may be normal.
source: Generated from 9. Gastrointestinal.pdf - Pathology: Acute and chronic pancreatitis

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 61-year-old woman with acute gallstone pancreatitis develops progressive hypoxemia requiring mechanical ventilation, hypotension requiring vasopressors, and a rising creatinine. She has no known cardiac, pulmonary, or renal disease.
question: Which of the following best describes these complications?

options.text: Local complications: pseudocyst and abscess formation
Systemic organ failure: ALI/ARDS, shock, and renal failure
Hypocalcemia from calcium soap precipitation alone
Chronic pancreatic insufficiency with steatorrhea and diabetes
Ascending cholangitis with Reynolds pentad

explanation_correct: Severe acute pancreatitis can lead to systemic organ failure, including acute lung injury and ARDS, shock, and renal failure, in addition to local complications such as pseudocyst, abscess, necrosis, hemorrhage, and infection. This patient's hypoxemia, vasopressor requirement, and rising creatinine directly reflect those systemic complications. Hypocalcemia from calcium soap precipitation often coexists but does not itself explain respiratory and renal failure.

explanation_incorrect.A: Pseudocyst and abscess are local collections and do not account for hypoxemia, shock, and acute kidney injury.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hypocalcemia is a recognized complication but would not by itself cause the respiratory failure and shock seen here.
explanation_incorrect.D: Chronic insufficiency causes steatorrhea, vitamin deficiency, and diabetes over time, not acute multi-organ failure.
explanation_incorrect.E: Reynolds pentad describes cholangitis with jaundice, fever, right upper quadrant pain, altered mental status, and shock, not ARDS and renal failure from pancreatitis.

educationalObjective: Severe acute pancreatitis can cause systemic organ failure with ALI/ARDS, shock, and renal failure, distinct from local pseudocyst or abscess formation.
